{{Short description|Concept in commutative algebra}}
{{distinguish|text=[[Prime ideal]]}}

In [[mathematics]], specifically [[commutative algebra]], a proper [[Ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] <math>\mathfrak q</math> of a [[commutative ring]] <math>A</math> is said to be '''primary''' if whenever <math>xy</math> is an element of <math>\mathfrak q</math> then <math>x</math> or <math>y^n</math> is also an element of <math>\mathfrak q</math>, for some <math>n>0</math>. For example, in the [[ring of integers]] <math>\mathbb Z</math>, <math>(p^n)</math> is a primary ideal if <math>p</math> is a [[prime number]].

The notion of primary ideals is important in commutative [[ring theory]] because every ideal of a [[Noetherian ring]] has a [[primary decomposition]], that is, can be written as an intersection of finitely many primary ideals. This result is known as the [[Lasker–Noether theorem]]. Consequently,<ref>To be precise, one usually uses this fact to prove the theorem.</ref> an [[irreducible ideal]] of a Noetherian ring is primary.

Various methods of generalizing primary ideals to noncommutative rings exist,<ref>See the references to Chatters–Hajarnavis, Goldman, Gorton–Heatherly, and Lesieur–Croisot.</ref> but the topic is most often studied for commutative rings. Therefore, the rings in this article are assumed to be commutative rings with identity.

==Examples and properties==

* The definition can be rephrased in a more apparently symmetrical manner: a proper ideal <math>\mathfrak{q}</math> is primary if, whenever <math>x y \in \mathfrak{q}</math>, <math>x </math> or <math>y</math> are elements of <math>\mathfrak{q}</math>, or both <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> lie in <math>\sqrt{\mathfrak{q}}</math>, the [[radical of an ideal|radical]] of <math>\mathfrak{q}</math>; i.e., <math>xy\in\mathfrak{q}\implies(x\in\mathfrak{q})\lor(y\in\mathfrak{q})\lor((x\in\sqrt{\mathfrak{q}})\land (y\in\sqrt{\mathfrak{q}})).</math>
* A proper ideal <math>{\mathfrak q}</math> of <math>R</math> is primary if and only if every [[zero divisor]] in <math>R/{\mathfrak q}</math> is nilpotent.  (Compare this to the case of prime ideals, where <math>{\mathfrak p}</math> is prime if and only if every zero divisor in <math>R/{\mathfrak p}</math> is actually zero.)
* Any [[prime ideal]] is primary, and moreover an ideal is prime if and only if it is primary and [[semiprime ideal|semiprime]] (also called [[Radical of an ideal|radical ideal]] in the commutative case).
* Every primary ideal is [[primal ideal|primal]].<ref>For the proof of the second part see the article of Fuchs.</ref>
* If <math>{\mathfrak q}</math> is a primary ideal, then the [[Radical of an ideal|radical]] of <math>{\mathfrak q}</math> is necessarily a prime ideal <math>{\mathfrak p}</math>, and this ideal is called the [[associated prime ideal]] of <math>{\mathfrak q}</math>. In this situation, <math>{\mathfrak q}</math> is said to be '''<math>{\mathfrak p}</math>-primary'''.
** On the other hand, an ideal whose radical is prime is not necessarily primary: for example, if <math>R = k[x,y,z]/(x y - z^2)</math>, <math>\mathfrak{p} = (\overline{x}, \overline{z})</math>, and <math>\mathfrak{q} = \mathfrak{p}^2</math>, then <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> is prime and <math>\sqrt{\mathfrak{q}} = \mathfrak{p}</math>, but we have <math> \overline{x} \overline{y} = {\overline{z}}^2 \in \mathfrak{p}^2 = \mathfrak{q}</math>, <math>\overline{x} \not \in \mathfrak{q}</math>, and <math>{\overline{y}}^n \not \in \mathfrak{q}</math> for all <math>n>0</math>, so <math>\mathfrak{q}</math> is not primary.  The primary decomposition of <math>\mathfrak{q}</math> is <math>(\overline{x}) \cap ({\overline{x}}^2, \overline{x} \overline{z}, \overline{y})</math>; here <math>(\overline{x})</math> is <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>-primary and <math>({\overline{x}}^2, \overline{x} \overline{z}, \overline{y})</math> is <math>(\overline{x}, \overline{y}, \overline{z})</math>-primary.
*** An ideal whose radical is ''maximal'', however, is primary.
*** Every ideal  <math>{\mathfrak q}</math> with radical <math>{\mathfrak p}</math> ''is'' contained in a smallest <math>{\mathfrak p}</math>-primary ideal: all elements <math>a</math> such that <math>ax\in {\mathfrak q}</math> for some <math>x\notin {\mathfrak p}</math>. The smallest <math>{\mathfrak p}</math>-primary ideal containing <math>{\mathfrak p}^n</math> is called the <math>n</math>th '''[[Symbolic power of a prime ideal|symbolic power]]''' of <math>{\mathfrak p}</math>.
* If <math>{\mathfrak p}</math> is a maximal prime ideal, then any ideal whose radical is <math>{\mathfrak p}</math> is <math>{\mathfrak p}</math>-primary (and vice versa). In particular, a power of <math>{\mathfrak p}</math> or an ideal containing a power of <math>{\mathfrak p}</math> is <math>{\mathfrak p}</math>-primary. But a <math>{\mathfrak p}</math>-primary ideal need not be a power of <math>{\mathfrak p}</math> and need not contain a power of <math>{\mathfrak p}</math>; for example, the ideal <math>(x,y^2)</math> is <math>{\mathfrak p}</math>-primary for the ideal <math>{\mathfrak p}=(x,y)</math> in the ring <math>k[x,y]</math>, but is not a power of <math>{\mathfrak p}</math>; however, it contains <math>{\mathfrak p}^2</math>.
* If <math>A</math> is a [[Noetherian ring]] and <math>{\mathfrak p}</math> a prime ideal, then the kernel of <math>A \to A_{\mathfrak p}</math>, the map from <math>A</math> to the [[localization of a ring|localization]] of <math>A</math> at <math>{\mathfrak p}</math>, is the intersection of all <math>{\mathfrak p}</math>-primary ideals.<ref>Atiyah–Macdonald, Corollary 10.21</ref>
* If <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> is maximal, a finite nonempty product of <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>-primary ideals is <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>-primary but an [[infinite product]] of <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>-primary ideals may not be <math>\mathfrak p</math>-primary; since for example, in a Noetherian local ring with maximal ideal <math>\mathfrak m</math>, <math>\textstyle\bigcap_{n > 0} \mathfrak{m}^n = 0</math> ([[Krull intersection theorem]]) where each <math>\mathfrak{m}^n</math> is <math>\mathfrak{m}</math>-primary, for example the infinite product of the maximal (and hence prime and hence primary) ideal <math>m=\langle x,y \rangle</math> of the local ring <math>K[x,y]/\langle x^2, xy\rangle</math> yields the zero ideal, which in this case is not primary (because the zero divisor <math>y</math> is not nilpotent). In fact, in a Noetherian ring, a nonempty product of <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>-primary ideals <math>Q_i</math> is <math>\mathfrak{p}</math>-primary if and only if there exists some integer <math>n > 0</math> such that <math>\mathfrak{p}^n \subset \textstyle\bigcap_i Q_i</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Bourbaki|loc=Ch. IV, § 2, Exercise 3.}}</ref>

== Decomposition of ideals into primary ideals ==
The primary decomposition of ideals by the Lasker–Noether theorem may be seen as a generalization of the [[fundamental theorem of arithmetic]], which applies to the integers <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> and other [[Unique factorization domain|unique factorization domains]], to general Noetherian rings.  While the unique factorization of elements of a ring into the product of irreducible elements (up to units and reordering) fails in the general case, the Lasker–Noether theorem states that the ''ideals'' of a Noetherian ring do still have a type of "unique factorization": any ideal in a Noetherian ring can be written as an intersection of primary ideals of the ring in a ''[[primary decomposition]]'', and while these component primary ideals are not necessarily unique, the radicals of these components, the ''[[Associated prime|associated primes]]'' of the ideal, are unique up to reordering:
{{Math theorem
| math_statement = Let <math>A</math> be a commutative Noetherian ring and let <math>\mathfrak{a}</math> be an ideal of <math>A</math>. Then <math>\mathfrak{a}</math> may be written as the intersection of finitely many primary ideals; that is:

: <math>\mathfrak{a}=\bigcap _{i=1}^{n}\mathfrak{q}_{i} </math>

with each <math>\mathfrak{q}_i</math> primary. The expression of <math>\mathfrak{a}</math> in this way is said to be a ''primary decomposition'' of <math>\mathfrak{a}.</math>  Furthermore, if (1) the <math>\sqrt{\mathfrak{q}_i}</math>  are all distinct and (2) <math>\mathfrak{q}_i\nsupseteq \bigcap_{j\neq i} \mathfrak{q}_j</math> for each <math>i</math>, then the primary decomposition is said to be ''irredundant''.  Any primary decomposition can be reduced to an irredundant one, and, if the aforementioned primary decomposition of  <math>\mathfrak{a}</math> is irredundant, and

: <math>\mathfrak{a}=\bigcap _{i=1}^{n'}\mathfrak{q}'_{i} </math>

is another irredundant primary decomposition of <math>\mathfrak{a}</math>, then <math>n=n'</math> and <math>\sqrt{\mathfrak{q}_i}=\sqrt{\mathfrak{q}'_i}</math> for each <math>i,</math> after possibly reindexing the <math>\mathfrak{q}'_i.</math>
| name = Theorem (Lasker–Noether)
}}
